claims.claim: Hearing aids likely give a large improvement in hearing-related quality of life and listening ability in adults with mild to moderate loss.
claims.supporting_passage: We included 16 RCTs involving 2261 participants... The average age ranged from 58 to 83 years... For hearing-specific health-related quality of life (participation), there is likely to be a large difference favouring those wearing hearing aids over the control comparison (SMD -1.25...; 8 studies, 1683 participants; moderate-certainty evidence...). For listening ability, there is likely to be a large difference favouring those wearing hearing aids (SMD -1.28...; 5 studies, 622 participants; moderate-certainty evidence...)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults, mild to moderate loss / hearing aids / passive or active control / hearing QoL, listening / 4 weeks to 3 years
claims.safe_wording: In trials of adults with mild to moderate hearing loss, mostly in their 60s and 70s, hearing aids probably make a large difference to everyday listening and to how much hearing gets in the way of daily life.
claims.qualifications: Say 'probably'; 'large' is a standardised effect size, not a percentage; trials not blinded.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: General quality of life: only small, low-certainty benefit.

claims.claim: The review did not show clear effects on loneliness or working memory.
claims.supporting_passage: For loneliness, there may be little to no difference... (low-certainty evidence...). For working memory, the evidence is very uncertain... The review did not provide evidence that hearing aids were effective at improving loneliness or working memory
claims.safe_wording: The same trials did not show a clear effect on loneliness, and the evidence on memory is very uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Evidence gap, not proof of no effect.

claims.claim: People wait years between noticing hearing difficulty and getting aids; NHS aids are free.
claims.safe_wording: Do not state a waiting time or NHS cost.
claims.qualifications: Not searched to a verified source.

claims.claim: Sudden hearing loss should be assessed urgently, first separating a blocked or conductive cause from inner-ear/nerve loss; prompt management may improve recovery.
claims.supporting_passage: Prompt recognition and management of sudden sensorineural hearing loss may improve hearing recovery and patient quality of life... (KAS 1) Clinicians should distinguish sensorineural hearing loss from conductive hearing loss when a patient first presents with sudden hearing loss... (KAS 4)... audiometry as soon as possible (within 14 days of symptom onset)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with sudden hearing loss / US guideline
claims.safe_wording: Sudden hearing loss in one ear should be checked urgently, not assumed to be wax. A clinician first needs to tell whether the ear canal is blocked or the inner ear or nerve is affected.
claims.qualifications: NICE NG98 '24 hours, ENT or emergency department' wording was NOT opened (BMJ summary text inaccessible); use only as search-level context or omit. Tuning fork detail not verified.

claims.claim: Steroids may be offered early but their benefit is uncertain.
claims.supporting_passage: (KAS 8) Clinicians may offer corticosteroids as initial therapy... within 2 weeks of symptom onset. / The value of steroids in the treatment of idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss remains unclear / Systemic corticosteroids are widely used, however their value remains unclear.
claims.safe_wording: Steroid treatment is an option if started within about two weeks, though trials have not shown clearly that it works.

claims.claim: Age-related hearing loss mainly affects high pitches, making consonants inaudible.
claims.supporting_passage: Age-related hearing loss is typified by high-frequency threshold elevation and associated reductions in speech perception because speech sounds, especially consonants, become inaudible.
claims.safe_wording: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, and many consonants are high-pitched, so a person can hear that someone is talking but miss parts of words.

claims.claim: Speaking clearly helps more than volume; shouting distorts.
claims.supporting_passage: The average intelligibility difference between clear and conversational speech averaged across talker was found to be 17 percentage points. To a first approximation, this difference was independent of the listener, level, and frequency-gain characteristic.
claims.pico_timeframe: 5 listeners with sensorineural loss / clear vs conversational speech / nonsense sentences
claims.safe_wording: Speaking clearly and a little slower helped listeners with hearing loss understand more, and the gain held at different loudness levels.
claims.qualifications: 'Shouting distorts speech' and 'rephrase rather than repeat' were NOT found in an opened source; present as practical advice (judgement) or drop.

numbers.meaning: clear vs conversational speech intelligibility, 5 listeners

claims.claim: NICE recommends wax removal in primary care, but it is not a core obligation without commissioning; funding varies and many practices stopped; access hard for people with poor mobility.
claims.supporting_passage: Funding for treatment of impacted earwax is variable across clinical commissioning groups (CCGs). National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidance recommends ear wax removal should be performed in primary care,although without a commissioned service, GPs are under no obligation to do so. The funding for these additional services is variable by CCG area, with many practices now opting out of providing irrigation due to cost, high service demand, and safety implications... This presents problems for access, particularly in patient populations who have mobility issues and rely on carers
claims.safe_wording: In England, NICE says wax removal should be done in primary care, but GP practices are not obliged to provide it unless it is commissioned locally, so access varies from area to area.
claims.qualifications: Source 2020 (CCG era); RNID 2025 figures (8.1 million without NHS service) are search_extract only; do not use. Do not blame GPs.

claims.claim: Impacted wax is common in care homes and removal improves hearing; hearing aid users at risk.
claims.supporting_passage: Nineteen participants (65.5%) had cerumen in at least one ear. Following cerumen removal, hearing improved in 80% of impacted ears compared with 3% of nonimpacted ears / 57% of participants showed excess cerumen requiring removal / Clinicians should perform otoscopy to detect the presence of cerumen in patients with hearing aids
claims.pico_timeframe: Care home residents over 65 (US n=29; Australia n=51)
claims.safe_wording: Small studies in care homes found wax needing removal in more than half of residents, and hearing improved in most blocked ears after removal. Guidelines say to check the ears of hearing aid users for wax.

numbers.meaning: ears with improved hearing, impacted vs non-impacted, 29 residents

claims.claim: Sensory loss lowers MoCA pass rates even after score adjustment.
claims.supporting_passage: Many standardized measures of cognition include items that must be seen or heard... More participants with normal sensory acuity passed the MoCA compared to those with sensory loss, even after modifying scores to adjust for sensory factors.
claims.safe_wording: In 301 older adults, people with hearing or sight loss passed the MoCA less often, even after adjusting scores for items they could not hear or see.
claims.qualifications: Association; could also reflect true cognitive differences.

claims.claim: Amplification during testing restores MoCA scores.
claims.supporting_passage: We did not find any effect of amplification or test modality on the total score of the cognitive screening test (i.e., MoCA). Amplification improved working memory performance as measured by word recall / the use of amplification did not significantly change performance... this should not be taken to suggest the use of amplification during testing is unnecessary
claims.safe_wording: Small studies found amplification did not change total MoCA scores, though it helped word recall; use aids anyway and record what was used.
claims.qualifications: Recording adaptations is judgement/good practice, not a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Directly conflicts with an implied promise that adaptations fix scores.

candidates.reason: High-frequency/consonant claim supported (Aydelott). Clear-over-loud supported only by tiny Picheny 1985; 'shouting distorts' and 'rephrase' not found in opened source.
candidates.revised_angle: Explain high-pitch loss and consonants; advise getting attention, facing the person and speaking clearly rather than louder; present rephrasing as practical advice, not a finding.

candidates.reason: Urgency and uncertain steroid benefit supported (AAO-HNS 2019, Cochrane). NICE NG98 24-hour wording not opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Sudden one-ear hearing loss needs urgent same-day assessment, not wax drops; cite AAO-HNS (separate blocked ear from inner-ear loss; steroids an option within 2 weeks with uncertain benefit). Add NICE 24-hour wording only if a later batch opens it.

candidates.reason: Editor's reworded access claim supported by Radford 2020 full text; Sharvill letter title only; RNID only search extract. Care-home prevalence from small studies.
candidates.revised_angle: Wax removal is not a core GP obligation in England unless locally commissioned, and access varies; NICE says do it in primary care; ask the practice where NHS wax removal is provided locally. No RNID numbers.

candidates.reason: Cochrane 2026 abstract supports benefit and null findings; drop waiting-time and NHS-cost claims.
Dupuis supported, but trials show amplification did not change total MoCA score; must not imply adaptations fix scores.
candidates.revised_angle: Check hearing aids in, glasses, quiet room, large print; record adaptations with the score because sensory loss is linked to lower MoCA pass rates and adaptations may not fully correct it.
